_podcast.theme_scoring_prompt:
Rate how well this article fits the theme 'Indigenous Lands & Innovation' — Indigenous nations using technology, governance, and stewardship on their own terms.

OUT OF SCOPE — score 0-9: geopolitical and war news with no Indigenous rights angle; general wildfire and wildlife-service updates not led by or directly affecting Indigenous communities or guardians; provincial forestry and environmental policy with no explicit First Nations involvement; consumer tech and gadget reviews; science with no Indigenous stewardship or sovereignty context; crime and judicial news unrelated to Indigenous rights.

CALIBRATION — apply this ladder to everything else. Indigenous-led journalism on governance, rights, and self-determination is a strong fit on its own: a technology hook raises a score but is NOT required to reach the top band.
- 80-100: Excellent Indigenous-led reporting. Cariboo stories bridging governance or culture AND technology land here (Tŝilhqot'in/Secwépemc/Dakelh language revitalization tech, guardian programs using sensors and drones, GIS land mapping, Indigenous-led connectivity, digital heritage projects) — and so does outstanding national coverage of sovereignty, treaty, and land rights.
- 55-79: Solid pan-Canadian Indigenous governance, sovereignty, land rights, treaty, or reconciliation journalism — APTN, Eagle Feather News, or IndigiNews-style coverage of First Nations governance, MMIWG, land claims, self-determination, and Indigenous-led services. Most Indigenous governance journalism belongs HERE, not below.
- 30-54: Indigenous cultural, community, or human-interest stories (awards, events, ceremonies) with limited governance substance, or BC land-stewardship and environmental stories with meaningful First Nations involvement.
- 10-29: General BC land, environmental, or forestry stories that mention Indigenous communities only in passing.

ANCHORS: 'Tŝilhqot'in Nation launches drone-based caribou monitoring on title lands' → 98. 'First Nations leaders reject BC's revised land-title framework' → 75. 'Secwépemc language app reaches 1,000 learners' → 88. 'BC Wildfire Service updates evacuation alerts for the Interior' → 8.

Score 0-100 where 100 is a perfect thematic match and 0 is completely unrelated.

items.title: [Fast Company] Entry-level tech jobs in NYC are being cut in half by the AI boom
items.content_html:
🪶 ✏️

At first glance, the tech scene in New York City appears to be thriving: OpenAI and Anthropic have been putting down roots in the city, while stalwarts of the tech industry like Google now have more than 14,000 employees based in New York. Between 2008 and 2023, tech employment in the city has increased 160%, outdone only by the explosive growth of the tech industry in San Francisco.

But overall job growth in NYC’s tech industry has stagnated in recent years, and there is one area in particular that has experienced a sharp dip: Entry-level tech jobs have taken a significant hit in the years since ChatGPT’s public release ushered in the AI boom. 

A new report from the Center for an Urban Future (CUF), a New York-based think tank, found that as of 2022, the number of entry-level job postings in the tech industry has dropped 49%—a bigger decline than in any other sector, even as generative AI has seemingly derailed entry-level hiring across sectors. There continues to be a steady supply of college graduates with computer science degrees, but there aren’t nearly enough entry-level positions available to them. 

“The core issue is that employers face an individual incentive to hire workers who already have two or three years of experience,” Eli Dvorkin, editorial and policy director at CUF and one of the authors of the report, said in a recent interview with Searchlight. “But if every employer acts that way, the broader entry-level ecosystem collapses, which ultimately harms employers as well.”

The analysis found that on the whole, the jobs that have seen a marked dip in hiring are those that are most exposed to generative AI. Since 2022, entry-level job postings in roles with high AI exposure have decreased 29% across New York City. 

The outlook is not quite as grim across other jobs: Entry-level hiring has remained robust—growing 21%—for jobs that are not especially exposed to AI, according to the CUF report. Even within tech, employers have continued hiring for roles that require expertise in security and data analysis. Entry-level workers with strong AI skills are in particularly high demand, and job postings have actually climbed 20% in over the past four years. 

Still, the overall decline in hiring for entry-level tech jobs echoes a broader shift in New York: Since 2022, most industries have seen a steady drop in job postings for entry-level roles. 

This hiring slump is representative of a broader phenomenon playing out across the country, particularly in sectors like tech and finance. Some economists have been wary about overstating the impact of generative AI on the labor force—and even high-profile AI leaders have walked back their bold claims about AI ushering in widespread job losses. 

But there are clear signs that entry-level workers are bearing the brunt of the toll: Stanford University’s Institute for Human-Centered Artificial Intelligence recently found that the employment gap for young workers (defined as workers ages 22 to 25) has widened in the last year to 19%, when compared against similarly situated workers in roles that are less exposed to AI. 

In a recent survey by the Pew Research Center, young workers were more skeptical of AI than they had been previously, a sign that they are increasingly concerned about how the fast-developing technology might upend the labor market. Nearly three-quarters of adults younger than 30 said they believe AI will reduce the number of jobs within the next two decades.

The reports of looming job losses often focus on how generative AI is impacting white-collar workers, but research from the Brookings Institution earlier this year indicates that it’s not just highly skilled candidates who are being shut out of the workforce. AI adoption is also disrupting the pathways available to people without college degrees who have traditionally been able to move into white-collar work. 

In cities like New York, the growth in tech employment has in the past helped many workers from low-income backgrounds move into more lucrative jobs—but the changes ushered in by AI may make it more difficult for those types of workers to find their footing. Those pathways could disappear altogether if the city doesn’t reinvest in its tech workforce and help New Yorkers get the experience they need to land the entry-level jobs that are in high demand. 

As Dvorkin put it recently: “If anything, our tech sector has proven remarkably resilient given all these macroeconomic changes and technology shifts, and it remains well-positioned for future growth. However, the real challenge is who gets the opportunity to enter that sector in the first place.”

items.title: [Fast Company] A CEO tried a 4-day week—but stopped after employees were secretly working on Fridays
items.content_html:
🪶 ✏️

When Austin-based workforce management company Safeguard Global piloted a four-day workweek in 2023, the goal was to improve recruitment and retention. 

After initially looking like a success, however, the experiment ran into problems. Some employees often worked late to preserve Friday as an “off day.” Others used Friday to secretly catch up on work. And some who strictly adhered to a four-day schedule felt like they were falling behind. 

It was “not the culture we wanted to create,” Safeguard Global CEO and founder Bjorn Reynolds recently told Fortune. 

Safeguard Global has since pivoted to giving its roughly 1,000 workers the option to choose their own working hours and days, which Reynolds described as a culture of “freedom and choice.” 

“Choose the hours that fit best for the work product you need,” he said. “If you can do that in four days, great; if you do it in five [days], but you’re taking two half days, whatever works for you.”

In recent years, the four-day workweek has moved from a fringe idea to a serious workplace experiment, joining return-to-office (RTO) mandates and flexible work among the most hotly debated issues in the post-pandemic workplace. 

Supporters point to evidence showing that a four-day workweek can improve employee well-being, increase productivity, and even improve tech adoption. A growing number of companies in the U.S. and Europe have experimented with shorter workweeks, many of whom have continued the arrangement beyond the original trial. The idea seems to be particularly popular with Gen Z workers, and has started to gain traction with policymakers. 

However, the four-day workweek is still far away from replacing the five-day workweek in the United States. And experiences like Safeguard Global’s show that the jury is still out on whether it is truly effective.

Safeguard’s walked-back experiment led Reynolds to believe that managers  should focus more on outcomes than hours. The company monitors its workers using three performance metrics, which vary by role. 

The key, Reynolds says, is making sure employees understand how the metrics feed into the company’s larger goals. 

“How does everybody’s daily productivity or daily outcomes ladder up to part of a broader initiative?” he said. “We really make sure you understand what you do is super critical and where you’re placed in the organization.”

The metrics also allow managers to identify potential areas for improvement.

“If someone’s customers are raising more than average tickets, and we’re not answering them, and the time to answer is longer than the average, it gives you the ability to then say, ‘Okay, well, hey, here’s an anomaly,” he said. “Maybe it’s your working patterns leading to that.”

items.title: [ArchDaily] Asmara Heritage Project: Documenting a Colonial Project that Became Eritrea's National Symbol
items.content_html:
🪶 ✏️

Asmara, the capital of Eritrea, sits at over 2,300 meters above sea level on a plateau at the edge of the Great Rift Valley escarpment. Although situated in a country not known for large visitor numbers, the city has gained fame for its unique architecture. In July 2017, it became a UNESCO World Heritage Site, inscribed as "Asmara: A Modernist African City," the first modernist urban site anywhere to be listed in its entirety, and Africa's first explicitly modernist World Heritage Site. Its heritage value came about as a result of a complex convergence of two aspects of Eritrea's history: an intense period of colonial construction as Italy pursued its imperial ambitions in Africa, and a long period of relative isolation that insulated the city from redevelopment.
